faqs.q: Will you relocate the iguanas on my Fort Lauderdale seawall?
faqs.a: No — relocation is off the table by law. The green iguana is a Prohibited nonnative species in Florida: captured animals cannot be released or moved to another location, and keeping one alive requires a permit. FWC encourages humane removal of iguanas from private property with the landowner's permission, which is the service we provide, followed by practical changes — trimming seawall vegetation, protecting young ornamentals, and removing fallen fruit — so new iguanas do not simply replace the ones removed.

Fort Lauderdale.wildlife_intro:
Fort Lauderdale's canal grid — the Venice of America layout — means most homes here sit a few feet from water, and the wildlife knows it. Green iguanas, a Prohibited species under Florida's Chapter 68-5 rules, bask on seawalls and strip ornamentals in the Las Olas and Coral Ridge neighborhoods; roof rats travel the canal-side palms; raccoons den in the attics of older Wilton Manors and Victoria Park houses. Muscovy ducks claim community ponds, and in the western suburbs Burmese python sightings, while uncommon, are handled as an FWC program matter, not a routine booking.

Iguana work in Fort Lauderdale is removal only — captured iguanas may never be relocated or released, and live possession is permit-gated, so the honest service is humane removal from your property plus habitat changes that make the seawall less inviting. For the attic animals, we pair trapping with tile-roof exclusion built for a canal climate. Reach us at (844) 544-3498 with a description or photo and we will tell you plainly which category your animal falls into.

faqs.q: What do I do about Muscovy ducks around my Hollywood home?

Traps are checked at least every 24 hours and any non-target bird is released on site. We will explain the lawful options for your property before any work starts.

faqs.q: What is scratching in my Miramar attic at night?

Miramar stretches from the older blocks near the Turnpike to the big western developments of Sunset Lakes and Riviera Isles, ending at the Everglades levee. Bat colonies in the tile roofs here are Brazilian free-tailed bats; exclusion is planned for the August 15 to April 15 legal window, with summer calls handled as inspection, partial sealing, and scheduling so the maternity colony is never trapped inside.

faqs.q: There is a small owl in a burrow on the lot next door in Coral Springs — can it be moved?
faqs.a: No. That is a Florida burrowing owl, a State Threatened species, and its burrow is protected — moving the bird or disturbing the burrow requires an FWC permit, which is a developer and agency process, not a homeowner service. Give the burrow space, keep dogs leashed near it, and let the owls be; after heavy rain they sometimes shelter briefly in eaves and return to the burrow on their own. If construction is planned near the burrow, contact FWC's gopher tortoise and burrowing owl permitting staff before any ground is disturbed.

Coral Springs.wildlife_intro:
Coral Springs was master-planned from the start — wide boulevards, strict landscaping, and neighborhoods like The Hills and Eagle Trace built around golf courses, lakes, and the Sawgrass Nature Center's green space. The planning did not keep wildlife out: raccoons den in chimneys of the 1970s original sections, iguanas graze the canal banks and golf-course edges, roof rats move through the mature ficus canopy, and burrowing owls occasionally claim a vacant lot — those are State Threatened, protected, and a permitting conversation, never a removal.

Golf-course adjacency shapes many Coral Springs calls. Animals commute from fairway rough and lake edges into the nearest attics, so we scope the whole roofline and the lot's tree contact, not just the active hole. Native animals we live-capture are handled under Rule 68A-9.010's clock and conditions — released on site or within Broward County on 40-plus acres with written permission, within 24 hours — and iguanas, as a Prohibited species, are removed, never relocated.

faqs.q: Rats are getting into my Davie barn feed — how do you handle that?
faqs.a: Feed storage is a magnet, so we start with the food: metal-lidded bins and a swept feed room remove most of the draw before a trap is set. Then we trap the rats using the structure and seal the barn's gaps — eave openings, slab cracks, door sweeps — because a barn that stays open will refill. Our work is nonchemical trapping and exclusion; if droppings are inside the house itself, that structure work follows the FDACS Chapter 482 boundary, and we will explain which credential applies before anyone starts.

Davie.wildlife_intro:
Davie kept its western-town character: equestrian trails, pasture fences, acre-plus lots, and neighborhoods where barns and hay sheds stand behind the houses. That rural texture changes the call sheet — raccoons and opossums in feed rooms, rats in tack and grain storage, armadillos under barn slabs, and snakes around pond edges and manure piles draw the questions here more than attic work, though the eastern subdivisions still produce plenty of roof rats and iguanas along the canals.

Outbuildings are the priority in Davie inspections. A sealed house means little if the feed room stays open, so we walk the whole property, prioritize the structures animals actually use, and set a trapping and exclusion plan sized to acreage rather than a suburban lot. Skunks under sheds get identified first — the striped skunk is the routine case, while a spotted skunk sighting is confirmed carefully before any trap is placed, since that species is a conservation concern in Florida.

faqs.q: What is digging the small sand mounds in my Plantation yard?
faqs.a: That depends on the shape. Eastern moles leave raised surface tunnels and small molehills, armadillos leave scattered digging in beds and lawn edges, and in sandy north and central Florida soils a southeastern pocket gopher leaves a row of sand mounds. A large burrow with a wide, half-moon apron of sand is different — that is likely a gopher tortoise burrow, which is protected, carries a 25-foot permit buffer, and must be left alone. Call us and describe the digging and we will identify it before any work is planned.
